notes.meaning: Jesus answers the religious leaders with a question of his own about John the Baptist. If they give him an honest answer, he promises to explain who gave him his authority. Countering a question with another question was a common and fair way to debate at that time.

Jesus asks whether John's baptism came from God in heaven or just from ordinary men. The leaders talk it over among themselves and see the trap. If they say John came from God, Jesus will ask why they refused to believe John's message and his witness about Jesus.

The leaders also realize they cannot say John's work was merely human. They are terrified of what the crowd will do, because the ordinary people firmly believe John was a true prophet from God. Their fear of people matters far more to them than telling the truth.

The leaders choose to pretend they do not know the answer rather than admit the truth. Because they refuse to be honest about John, Jesus refuses to tell them by what authority he acts. When people deliberately reject the light God has already shown them, Jesus gives them no further explanation.

Jesus tells a story about a father who tells his first son to go and work in his vineyard. The vineyard represents God's kingdom and the service God calls people to do. Jesus asks his hearers to judge this everyday picture so they will examine their own lives.

The first son rudely refuses to obey his father at first, openly saying no. Later on, he feels regret, changes his mind, and actually goes to work. This son pictures openly sinful people who begin by defying God but later turn to him in genuine repentance.

The father gives the exact same command to the second son, who answers politely and promises to go right away. Yet in reality, he never goes into the vineyard at all. This son represents self-righteous people who make loud religious promises but never obey God with their actions.

When Jesus asks which son obeyed the father, the leaders rightly say the first one did. Jesus then shocks them by saying that despised tax collectors and prostitutes are entering God's kingdom ahead of them. Those outcasts had lived wicked lives, but they turned to God when they heard the good news.

John the Baptist came preaching God's call to repentance and living an upright life, but the religious leaders refused to believe him. Meanwhile, notorious sinners repented and trusted John's message. Even after seeing those changed lives with their own eyes, the leaders remained stubborn and refused to believe.

Jesus tells another story about a landowner who plants a vineyard, equips it with a wall, winepress, and watchtower, and leases it out to tenant farmers. This parable borrows imagery from Isaiah to show how richly God provided for Israel and trusted its leaders to care for his people.

When the harvest arrives, the owner sends his servants to collect his agreed share of the fruit. In Bible times, rent was often paid using part of the crop. These servants represent the prophets whom God sent throughout history to call his people to bear fruits of obedience.

The tenants violently seize the owner's servants, beating one, killing another, and stoning a third. This terrible abuse pictures how Israel's leaders repeatedly mistreated God's true messengers. God's prophets were often mocked, hurt, and put to death simply for speaking his words.

The owner patiently sends a second group with even more servants, but the tenants treat them with the same cruelty. This shows God's extraordinary patience over many centuries as he continued to reach out to his people. Instead of softening, the leaders grew more hardened against God.

Finally, the owner sends his own beloved son, expecting the tenants to show him proper respect. This marks the peak of God's message to humanity. God sent his only Son, Jesus Christ, who stands far higher in authority and honor than any prophet before him.

When the tenants spot the son, they plot among themselves to murder him so they can take the property for themselves. This pictures the corrupt Jewish authorities plotting to kill Jesus to keep their own power and position. In their blindness, they thought eliminating God's Son would leave them in control.

The tenants grab the son, drag him outside the vineyard, and kill him. This foretells how Jesus would be handed over to the Romans and crucified outside the walls of Jerusalem. It demonstrates how far human rebellion will go when rejecting God's rightful authority.

Jesus asks his hearers what the owner will do to those wicked tenants when he comes back. By asking this, Jesus causes the religious leaders to judge the case without realizing they are condemning themselves. God's standard of justice is so clear that even sinners must agree with it.

The listeners answer that the owner will bring those evil men to a terrible end and rent the vineyard to new tenants who will give him his fruit. With this answer, the leaders pronounce their own coming punishment. God's blessings would be taken from them and given to leaders who will serve him faithfully.

Jesus quotes Psalm 118 about a stone thrown away by builders that God chose to make the chief cornerstone. A cornerstone was the vital stone that held up and aligned the whole building. Though Israel's spiritual builders rejected Jesus, God made him the supreme foundation of his church.

Jesus plainly warns that the kingdom of God will be taken from those corrupt leaders and given to a people who produce its fruit. This refers to the church of believers, made up of both Jews and Gentiles, who trust and obey Christ. God demands lives that bear the fruit of the Spirit rather than empty religion.

Anyone who trips over this stone will be broken, but anyone on whom the stone falls will be crushed into dust. Rejecting Jesus brings spiritual damage right now, and facing his final judgment brings complete destruction. God's appointed Savior cannot be opposed without fatal results.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars observe that certain early Greek manuscripts leave this verse out, suggesting it may have been copied over from Luke's Gospel.

notes.meaning: When the chief priests and Pharisees hear these parables, they finally understand that Jesus is talking about them. The stories pull off their disguise and clearly expose their rebellion against God. Instead of leading them to repent, the truth only makes them furious.

The leaders want to arrest Jesus right on the spot, but they hold back out of fear because the crowds view him as a prophet. Their fear of the people keeps their violent hatred in check for the moment. Even in their anger, evil men can do nothing beyond what God allows.
